data.title: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
data.description: From 65,000 years of continuous First Nations custodianship and Captain Cook’s voyage to the First Fleet, frontier wars, convict labour, the Gold Rush, and Aboriginal resistance, investigate how colonisation built modern Australia through dispossession and struggle.
data.synopsis: Sixty-five thousand years of the world's oldest continuous living culture collided in 1788 with eleven British convict ships casting anchor in Sydney Cove. Step beyond the colonial myth of terra nullius to discover the profound cosmology, complex diplomatic systems, and sophisticated fire-stick land management of First Nations peoples. Confront the brutal realities of convict transportation, the iron-fisted governance of penal colonies, and the fierce resistance of warriors like Pemulwuy during the Frontier Wars. From the blood-soaked Black War in Van Diemen's Land and the miners' democratic insurrection at the Eureka Stockade to the birth of a federated Commonwealth in 1901—explore the enduring story of invasion, resistance, and unbroken Indigenous survival.
data.enquiry: Invasion, Settlement, or Survival? How did British colonisation transform Australia?

data.title: The First British Empire (1600–1783)
data.description: From the founding of the East India Company and the horrors of the Transatlantic slave trade to Jamaican Maroon resistance and the American Revolution, explore how commercial greed, human exploitation, and colonial rebellion built and fractured the First British Empire.
data.synopsis: Armed merchantmen braving uncharted oceans, chartered monopolies extorting immense wealth from the Mughal Empire, and the catastrophic human horror of the Transatlantic Slave Trade. An isolated northern island built global dominion on ruthless commercial exploitation, sugar plantations drenched in blood, and forced labor across the Americas. Confront the reality of the Middle Passage, the fierce guerrilla defiance of Queen Nanny and Jamaican Maroons, and the explosive rebellion of the Thirteen Colonies—as tea was cast into Boston Harbor and George Washington shattered imperial rule to ignite the American Revolution.
data.enquiry: How did trade, slavery, and rebellion shape the First British Empire?

data.title: KS3: Causes of the Great War
data.synopsis: Decades of imperial vanity, naval rivalries, and rigid alliance treaties wound the clockwork of European catastrophe. From the blood and iron of German unification under Bismarck to the industrial race between British Dreadnoughts and Kaiser Wilhelm’s High Seas Fleet, Europe split into two heavily armed camps. When a teenage assassin fired two fatal shots in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, thirty days of diplomatic brinkmanship sleepwalked an entire continent into total war.
data.enquiry: How did decades of imperial rivalry and fear culminate in thirty days of madness?

data.title: KS3: The Great War — Apocalypse & Aftermath (1914–1919)
data.synopsis: When Europe plunged into the abyss in August 1914, millions of young men rushed to enlist in an adventure they believed would be over by Christmas. Instead, industrial machinery transformed warfare into unprecedented slaughter. Confront the muddy hell of trench warfare and the controversial decisions of British generals at the Somme, uncover the forgotten global sacrifice of colonial soldiers from across the Empire, examine how total war gripped the Home Front under DORA, and discover how the bitter compromises of the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 sowed the seeds of future catastrophe.
data.enquiry: How did total industrialised war (1914–1919) shatter societies and transform the modern world?

data.title: KS3: The Industrial Revolution (1750–1900)
data.synopsis: Steam engines shrieking in smoke-choked valleys, red-hot iron rolling through Henry Cort's puddling furnaces, and coal-fired textile mills driving the heartbeat of the modern world. Britain transformed from an agrarian island into the undisputed 'Workshop of the World', yet this unprecedented economic power was bought with human agony: child scavengers crawling beneath thunderous cotton looms, cholera epidemics stalking filthy back-to-back slums, and desperate handloom weavers smashing machinery. Follow the courageous struggle of millions of ordinary working people—from the bloodied field of Peterloo to the millions-strong petitions of the Chartists—who fought against the ruling elite to win the right to vote and forge modern British democracy.
data.enquiry: How did steam, factories, and the fight for democracy transform Britain?

data.title: Medieval England: 1066–1485
data.description: From the succession crisis of 1066 and Norman castle subjugation to the murder of Thomas Becket, Magna Carta, and the catastrophe of the Black Death, explore how military force, religious authority, and popular rebellion forged the medieval realm.
data.synopsis: A disputed succession, a blood-soaked hilltop in Sussex, and a conqueror's iron fist that violently transformed Anglo-Saxon England forever. Enter the tumultuous world of stone fortresses, feudal bondage, and royal fury. data.title: KS3: The Second British Empire (1783–1914)
data.description: From East India Company monopoly rule and Portsmouth Royal Dockyard to Australian settler colonialism, the 1857 Indian Rebellion, the Scramble for Africa, and Dadabhai Naoroji’s Drain Theory, explore how global commerce, naval power, dispossession, and armed resistance shaped the Second British Empire.
data.synopsis: A vast maritime empire painted red across world maps, propelled by ironclad warships, industrial machinery, and the relentless extraction of colonial wealth. From the bustling slipways of Portsmouth Royal Dockyard to the brutal suppression of the 1857 Indian Rebellion, Britain governed a fifth of humanity under the banner of imperial civilising mission. Confront the stark realities of conquest and displacement: the expansion of penal colonies into Indigenous Australia, the violent partition of the African continent during the Scramble for Africa, and the pioneering economic critique of Dadabhai Naoroji exposing how Britain drained trillions from the Indian subcontinent.

data.subtitle: Understanding the Holocaust: How and Why Did it Happen?
data.synopsis: Before the catastrophic rupture of the Second World War, over nine million Jewish people inhabited every corner of Europe, speaking dozens of languages and enriching the intellectual, artistic, and political fabric of the continent. Trace how Adolf Hitler and the Nazi regime systematically weaponized racial antisemitism to strip German Jews of civil rights and legal personhood, before exploiting the smoke and chaos of total war to engineer the continent-wide annihilation of six million human beings. From the claustrophobic terror of the Warsaw Ghetto and the secret chronicle of the Ringelblum Archive to the mass shootings of the Einsatzgruppen in the killing fields of Ukraine, the industrial extermination machinery of Auschwitz-Birkenau, and the armed heroism of ghetto fighters and righteous rescuers—confront the deepest moral questions of complicity, indifference, human resistance, and the enduring obligation to remember.

data.title: Paper 3: Conflict at Home and Abroad: the USA, 1954–75
data.synopsis: Torn apart by two simultaneous existential struggles, the United States fought a ferocious battle for its own soul at home and abroad. On the domestic front, Black Americans risked their lives against Jim Crow terror, police dogs, and disenfranchisement—advancing from the legal triumph of Brown v. Topeka and MLK's non-violent marches to the fiery radicalism of Malcolm X and Black Power. Simultaneously, deep in the Southeast Asian jungle, over 500,000 conscripted GIs waged a brutal counter-insurgency against resilient Vietcong guerrillas. As napalm, the 1968 Tet Offensive, and the My Lai massacre were beamed into American living rooms, anti-war protests, student strikes, and the Kent State shootings fractured the nation, culminating in painful withdrawal and the fall of Saigon in 1975.
data.enquiry_question: Civil Rights and the Vietnam War: How did social and foreign crises transform the USA?

lessons.title: KT 1.1: What was the position of Black Americans in the early 1950s?
lessons.enquiry: In the early 1950s, Black Americans in the Southern states lived under the oppressive system of Jim Crow. Racial segregation was legally enforced by state laws, and voting rights were systematically denied through arbitrary tests and economic terror. To fight this institutionalised inequality, civil rights organisations deployed different strategies: the NAACP used legal litigation in federal courts, while CORE pioneered non-violent direct action protests. How did legal challenges and grassroots direct action begin to erode the entrenched system of Southern segregation?

lessons.title: KT 1.2: How did developments in education challenge segregation (1954–57)?
lessons.enquiry: The desegregation of public schools became the first major battleground of the civil rights movement. In 1954, the NAACP won the landmark Brown v. Board of Education case, with the Supreme Court declaring school segregation unconstitutional. However, this sparked 'Massive Resistance' across the South, culminating in the Little Rock High School crisis in 1957. Here, Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus defied federal law, forcing President Eisenhower to deploy federal troops to protect Black students. Why did the desegregation of Little Rock Central High School force the federal government to intervene directly in the South?

lessons.title: KT 1.3: How did the Montgomery Bus Boycott happen, and why did it succeed?
lessons.enquiry: The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956) was the first major grassroots test of non-violent resistance. Beginning immediately after Rosa Parks' arrest on 1 December 1955, the local Black community organized the Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA), electing Martin Luther King Jr. as president. Black citizens, who made up 70% of bus riders, walked, carpooled, and organized private cabs for 381 days. Despite bombings, arrests, and intimidation, the boycott devastated bus revenues until November 1956, when the Supreme Court ruled segregated transport unconstitutional, proving the power of mass direct action. Why was the Montgomery Bus Boycott successful, and how did it establish non-violent mass protest as a central civil rights strategy?

lessons.title: KT 1.4: Why did white people in the South resist integration, and how did they do it?
lessons.enquiry: In the wake of the 1954 Brown decision and the 1956 Montgomery victory, Southern white resistance hardened. Southern politicians signed the 'Southern Manifesto' in 1956, pledging to defeat integration by all legal means. Segregationists formed White Citizens' Councils, using economic retaliation, firings, and mortgage foreclosures against Black activists. Concurrently, KKK violence erupted, targeting leaders with bombings. Governors like Orval Faubus (1957) and later Ross Barnett (1962) used state forces to defy federal mandates, creating a constitutional crisis over states' rights. How and why did Southern segregationists resist integration, and why did this create a constitutional crisis between state and federal authorities?

lessons.title: KT 2.1: How did peaceful protests (like sit-ins and Freedom Rides) force the government to act?
lessons.enquiry: By 1960, a new generation of student activists accelerated the movement. In February 1960, four Black students staged a sit-in at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, launching a wave of sit-ins that integrated over 100 lunch counters. In May 1961, the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) launched the Freedom Rides to test desegregation on interstate buses, facing brutal mob violence and bombings in Alabama. In September 1962, James Meredith became the first Black student at the University of Mississippi, requiring federal marshals and troops to suppress a segregationist riot that left two dead. How did student sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and campus integrations escalate pressure on the federal government to act?

lessons.title: KT 2.2: How did protests in Birmingham and Selma lead to the Civil and Voting Rights Acts?
lessons.enquiry: In 1963 and 1965, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) targeted the most segregated cities. The Birmingham Campaign (April 1963) saw police chief Bull Connor use fire hoses and attack dogs on child protesters, sparking international outrage and forcing President Kennedy to draft civil rights legislation. Following the Civil Rights Act of 1964, attention shifted to voting. In March 1965, the Selma-to-Montgomery marches faced state trooper violence on 'Bloody Sunday', forcing President Johnson to pass the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which outlawed literacy tests. How did national television coverage of police brutality in Birmingham and Selma shock the American public and compel Congress to pass civil rights legislation?

lessons.title: KT 2.3: What was the Black Power movement, and how did it differ from non-violent protests?
lessons.enquiry: By the mid-1960s, frustration with slow progress and continued white violence led to a major ideological split. Malcolm X, representing the Nation of Islam, criticized MLK's integrationist non-violence and championed Black nationalism and self-defense 'by any means necessary'. Following Malcolm's 1965 assassination, Stokely Carmichael popularised the term 'Black Power' at a 1966 march. This philosophy was institutionalized by the Black Panther Party (founded 1966), which organized armed neighborhood patrols and community programs, reflecting a shift toward racial pride and economic independence. Why did the Black Power movement emerge in the mid-1960s, and how did its methods and philosophy differ from non-violent direct action?

lessons.title: KT 2.4: Why did riots break out in American cities between 1965 and 1968?
lessons.enquiry: Between 1965 and 1967, deep-seated grievances over poverty, housing, and police brutality triggered massive urban riots in Northern and Western cities, including Watts (1965) and Detroit (1967). In response, President Johnson established the Kerner Commission, which reported in 1968 that America was moving toward 'two societies, one Black, one white—separate and unequal', blaming systemic white racism. Following Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination in April 1968, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (Fair Housing Act), prohibiting racial discrimination in housing. Why did violent urban riots erupt in northern and western cities between 1965 and 1968, and what did they reveal about racial inequality beyond the South?

lessons.title: KT 3.1: Why did the US support the unpopular government of Ngo Dinh Diem in South Vietnam?
lessons.enquiry: Following the 1954 Geneva Accords, which temporarily divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, the United States committed to containing communism in Southeast Asia. Guided by President Eisenhower's 'Domino Theory'—the belief that if Vietnam fell to communism, neighboring nations would follow—the USA backed Ngo Dinh Diem's anti-communist government in South Vietnam. However, Diem's corrupt regime, Buddhist persecutions, and refusal to hold elections alienated the populace, leading to the 1960 formation of the Vietcong and Diem's ultimate assassination in November 1963. Why did the United States back the corrupt regime of Ngo Dinh Diem, and how did his overthrow deepen American involvement in Vietnam?

lessons.title: KT 3.2: Why did the US send combat troops to Vietnam after the Gulf of Tonkin incident?
lessons.enquiry: Following President Kennedy's assassination in 1963, President Johnson inherited a rapidly deteriorating situation in South Vietnam. In August 1964, reports of US destroyers being attacked by North Vietnamese patrol boats in the Gulf of Tonkin provided the pretext Johnson needed. Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, granting the president power to take 'all necessary measures' to repel attacks. In early 1965, Johnson launched Operation Rolling Thunder, a massive bombing campaign, and deployed the first US combat troops to Da Nang in March, escalating the conflict dramatically. How did the Gulf of Tonkin incident enable President Johnson to commit US ground combat troops to the war in Vietnam?

lessons.title: KT 3.3: Why did US military tactics (like bombing and search & destroy) fail to defeat the Vietcong?
lessons.enquiry: Between 1965 and 1968, the Vietnam War became a brutal conflict of contrasting strategies. The US military, led by General Westmoreland, relied on high-tech attrition tactics, including 'Search and Destroy' missions, massive carpet bombing, and chemical agents like Agent Orange and Napalm to clear jungles and crop cover. In contrast, the Vietcong fought a guerrilla war, avoiding pitched battles, hiding in complex underground tunnel networks, and deploying deadly booby traps, which neutralized US technological superiority and severely damaged US soldier morale. Why did advanced American military tactics, such as Operation Rolling Thunder and search-and-destroy missions, fail to break the Vietcong?

lessons.title: KT 3.4: What was Nixon's 'Vietnamization' policy, and did it achieve peace with honour?
lessons.enquiry: Elected in 1968 on a promise of 'Peace with Honor', President Nixon sought to reduce US involvement without appearing to surrender. In 1969, he introduced 'Vietnamization'—a policy to train and equip the South Vietnamese army (ARVN) to take over combat operations, allowing the gradual withdrawal of US troops. However, to disrupt communist supply lines along the Ho Chi Minh Trail, Nixon secretly ordered the bombing and invasion of neighboring Cambodia (1970) and Laos (1971), expanding the war geographic scale and triggering massive protests at home. What was the strategy behind Nixon's policy of 'Vietnamization', and why did the secret expansion into Cambodia and Laos provoke intense domestic fury?

lessons.title: KT 4.1: Why did so many Americans oppose the Vietnam War (like at My Lai and Kent State)?
lessons.enquiry: As the war dragged on, domestic opposition erupted into a powerful movement. The introduction of the draft in 1965 and the first televised war brought graphic footage of civilian casualties directly into American living rooms, creating a 'credibility gap' between government claims and reality. The shock of the 1968 Tet Offensive and the 1969 exposure of the My Lai Massacre—where US troops murdered over 500 civilians—further fueled protests. Tension peaked in May 1970 at Kent State University, where National Guardsmen shot and killed four student protesters, polarizing the nation. Why did domestic opposition to the Vietnam War intensify so dramatically following the Tet Offensive, the My Lai revelations, and the Kent State shootings?

lessons.title: KT 4.2: Why did some Americans support the Vietnam War and the 'Silent Majority'?
lessons.enquiry: Despite the high profile of the anti-war movement, millions of Americans supported the war or opposed the protests. In November 1969, President Nixon appealed to the 'Silent Majority'—conservative, patriotic, working-class citizens who felt alienated by radical counterculture and anti-war demonstrations. Pro-war support was fueled by deep-seated anti-communism, respect for law and order, and the belief that protesting troops during wartime was unpatriotic. Nixon's strategy was highly successful, enabling him to secure a landslide re-election in 1972. Why did millions of Americans in the 'Silent Majority' continue to support the Vietnam War despite widespread anti-war demonstrations?

lessons.title: KT 4.3: How did the US exit Vietnam, and why did South Vietnam fall so quickly in 1975?
lessons.enquiry: Peace negotiations began in Paris in 1968 but remained deadlocked for years. In late 1972, Nixon ordered the devastating 'Christmas Bombings' of Hanoi to pressure North Vietnam. In January 1973, the Paris Peace Accords were signed, leading to the complete withdrawal of all US combat forces. However, fighting resumed between Vietnamese forces, and without US air support, the ARVN crumbled. In April 1975, communist forces launched the Spring Offensive, capturing the capital and renaming it Ho Chi Minh City, completing the reunification of Vietnam under communist rule. How did the United States negotiate its withdrawal under the Paris Peace Accords, and why did South Vietnam collapse so rapidly in 1975?

lessons.title: KT 4.4: What were the main reasons why the US failed to win the war in Vietnam?
lessons.enquiry: The failure of the USA to defeat communist forces in Vietnam was the result of interconnected military, political, and social factors. Militarily, the Vietcong's guerrilla tactics, local knowledge, and supplies from China and the USSR defeated US attrition strategies. Politically, the South Vietnamese government remained corrupt and unpopular, whereas the North Vietnamese exhibited absolute determination (the 'commitment bug'). Socially, the growing anti-war movement and draft resistance destroyed the domestic political support necessary to sustain a prolonged war, forcing US withdrawal. What was the decisive reason why the United States failed to achieve its military and political objectives in Vietnam?

data.title: KS3: Water and Sanitation Through Time
data.description: From Roman aqueducts and medieval cesspits to the Great Stink of 1858 and John Snow’s Broad Street pump, explore how two millennia of engineering triumphs, devastating epidemics, and scientific breakthroughs transformed public health in Britain.
data.synopsis: Two thousand years of human filth, deadly waterborne pestilence, and the desperate struggle for pure water. From Roman military engineers carving mountain aqueducts and baths to medieval monks engineering lead conduits against the Black Death, Britain's crowded cities were recurring death-traps. Follow the fearless visionaries—from John Snow mapping the Broad Street pump to Joseph Bazalgette blasting three hundred million bricks into the London subsoil to defeat the Great Stink—who conquered miasma theory and rebuilt public health from the sewers up.
data.enquiry: Why did it take so long to clean up Britain?
